extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (ethics), scholars studying Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Aristotle's account of friendship: its species, motives, requirements, functions, and political analogies as given in Nicomachean Ethics (Book VIII excerpts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as virtue or connected with virtue; necessary for life
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is either itself a virtue or connected with virtue, and it is necessary for life because no one would choose to live without friends even if he had all other good things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasizes practical value (friends enable and receive kindnesses, help preserve prosperity, and serve as refuge in poverty and adversity). Rich and powerful especially need friends because prosperity is 'slippery and hazardous'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of Friendship across life-stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship helps the young to keep from error, the old with attention and deficiencies, and those in their prime with devising and carrying out noble deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship provides corrective and supportive functions appropriate to different ages: instruction and correction for youth, assistance for the infirm, and cooperative action for adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural/instinctive basis of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship appears implanted in us by Nature (e.g., parent towards offspring, offspring towards parent, birds and animals showing similar ties, same-tribe and same-nation affinities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle cites biological and social examples to argue that friendly bonds have natural origins and are observable across species and human social groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as the bond of social communities; legislatorial priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is the bond of Social Communities, and legislators aim to secure it, sometimes even more than Justice; unanimity is akin to Friendship and faction is driven out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political life depends on friendship/unanimity; lawmakers structure institutions to promote friendly unity because it stabilizes communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship can replace justice among close associates
rubrics_metrics.description: Where people are in Friendship justice is not required; yet even the just need Friendship in addition, and the truly just partakes of the nature of Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes overlap and distinction: friendship can make formal justice unnecessary within close relations, but justice and friendship are complementary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is honourable and socially praised
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is not only necessary but honourable: we praise those fond of friends, and having numerous friends is regarded as a credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social recognition: being a friend (or having friends) is part of reputation and perceived moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate: does likeness or contrariety ground Friendship?
rubrics_metrics.description: Some say friendship arises from resemblance ('Like will to like'), others argue contrariety or opposition produces agreement; philosophers (Euripides, Heraclitus, Empedocles) propose different physical analogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes these physical theories but sets them aside as not central to the moral enquiry, while acknowledging the dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter of Friendship: good, pleasurable, or useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship's object is not everything indiscriminately but typically what is good, or pleasurable, or useful — three causes from which men feel Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes these as distinct motives/foci of affection and uses them to classify species of friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutuality and mutual knowledge as requirement for Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: To be friendship there must be kindly feelings toward one another, a wish for one another's good (from one of the three causes), and these kindly feelings should be mutually known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent mutual knowledge the relation is merely kindness or benevolence rather than full friendship; reciprocity and awareness complete the friendship relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three species of Friendship: utility, pleasure, and virtue (good)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships are three in number, corresponding to the objects (useful, pleasurable, good). Each species involves mutual affection mutually known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy is central: each species has different motivations, durability, and moral status; Aristotle repeatedly returns to these three kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility-based Friendship: contingent and instrumental
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have friendship for utility love their friends only insofar as some good arises to them; such friendships are result-based and liable to dissolution when advantage ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common among old or profit-seeking people; characterized by lack of intimacy and interchange of friendly actions except as means to advantage; hospitality often ranks here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure-based Friendship: passion-driven and transient
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship grounded in pleasure is common among the young, who pursue what is pleasurable and form/dissolve friendships rapidly as pleasures change; these friendships seek society and intimate intercourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often aligned with love and immediate impulses; intense social interaction is typical but stability is low as pleasures shift with age and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect (virtue-based) Friendship: mutual goodness and end in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Friendship subsists between those who are good and similar in goodness; they wish one another's good for the other's sake and the friendship is permanent as goodness has a principle of permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Aristotle's highest form: mutual, self-regarding insofar as each becomes a good to the other, mutually pleasurable and useful in an intrinsic way; rare and requires time and intimacy ('eat the requisite quantity of salt together').

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary friendships as resembling perfect friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships based on pleasure or profit are often called friends by analogy to the virtuous friendship, but are only friends 'in the way of result' rather than for the other's sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle allows common usage of 'friend' for these ties but stresses their ontological difference from true (virtue-based) friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability linked to sameness of result and source
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships are most permanent when the same result accrues to both and from the same source (e.g., two men of similar pleasantry), whereas asymmetrical result-sources (lover vs beloved) are less stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry of benefit and commonality of causes strengthen friendships; divergence produces instability when conditions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only the good can be friends disinterestedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad men may be friends for pleasure or profit, but only the good can be friends for one another's sake (disinterestedly), since bad men lack stable good and take pleasure only incidentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral character determines possibility of true friendship: stable virtue enables mutual wishing of good for the friend's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship resists calumny among the good
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship of the good is superior to calumny: men who have long tested one another have mutual confidence and do not easily believe third-party accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust and proven character produce resilience against slander; other kinds of friendship lack this protective depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship lies more in entertaining the sentiment than in being its object
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle claims 'Friendship stands rather in the entertaining, than in being the object of, the sentiment' — the excellence of friends is in feeling the friendship, not merely being its recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some mothers adopt and bear friendly feeling without requiring return; the inward state (moral disposition) matters more than external recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity and shared pleasure as conditions for Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Living together and taking pleasure in the same objects characterize friendship of companionship; long absence can cause forgetfulness and destroy friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance prevents the acting out of friendship and, when prolonged, erodes the relation; morose or elderly people are less apt to form friendships due to diminished pleasurableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited number of perfect friends
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not possible to be a perfect friend to many people simultaneously; perfect friendship is an excessive state naturally with but one object, though one may have many friends on grounds of advantage or pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True intimacy and deep mutual good require time and selective focus; lesser friendships can be more numerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and equality as ties; proportionality in superior-inferior friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality and similarity (especially similarity of goodness) are ties of Friendship; in relationships of superior and inferior the feeling should be in due proportion, producing a form of equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is great disparity of goodness, prosperity, or other qualities, friendship weakens. Proportionate feelings can make unequal parties friends by balancing affective relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire for honour vs entertaining friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Many desire to be objects of friendship (like honour) rather than to entertain friendship; some seek flatterers because being the object of friendly regard confers honour and perceived benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social motives can distort friendship: being esteemed by powerful people is instrumental, whereas true friends value entertaining the sentiment itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship and Justice co-extensive with forms of Communion
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship and Justice have the same object-matter and subsist between the same persons; Friendship is co-extensive with the various Communions (familial, civic, military) and corresponding principles of justice differ by degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses this to explain why 'the goods of friends are common' and why injustices are intensified when done to friends rather than strangers; political and social structures shape the scope of friendship and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political constitutions and their corruptions as analogues of social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three good political constitutions (Kingship/Monarchy, Aristocracy, Timocracy) and corresponding corruptions (Despotism, Oligarchy, Democracy respectively), with family/domestic relations exemplifying each type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle maps political forms to domestic relations: father-sons ~ Kingship, husband-wife ~ Aristocracy, brothers ~ Timocracy; departures from right rule produce the corrupt forms (e.g., master-slave as Despotism). This serves to relate friendship/justice patterns to political organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship between superior and inferior differs by role and expected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships between superior and inferior (father/son, ruler/ruled, husband/wife) are not identical: the work/excellence of each differs and so do causes and feelings; equitable friendship arises when proper duties are fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These friendships are correct when each party performs expected roles (children render due to authors of being; parents give maintenance and education); proportional justice and proportionate affection are required for permanence.
